title: The Most Confident Person in the Room Is Usually the Most Afraid
author: Kelly McGinnis
summary: Kelly McGinnis recounts a whiteboard moment when a company head wiped away her simple cash-runway arithmetic and told her to sit down, and says it took twenty years to realize he was terrified rather than powerful. She describes three difficult bosses, the founder, the perfectionist and the executive who rewrote her deck, who looked different but ran on the same fuel: fear of being found out hidden behind confidence. She argues that confidence and competence look identical from outside, so frightened people often rise, and that fear at the top is expensive because everyone below softens the truth. Secure leaders, by contrast, know the limits of what they know, hire people who will correct them, and can say I do not know, I was wrong, and you understand this better than I do. She explains that she left corporate life to own her own days.
points: Difficult bosses who seem powerful are often frightened, and their fear transfers to subordinates as self-doubt.
Confidence and competence are indistinguishable in a first impression, which helps explain why the wrong people rise.
When the most powerful person flinches from the truth, everyone below rearranges themselves and the organization starts softening reality.
A reliable test of a secure leader is whether they can say I do not know, I was wrong, and you understand this better than I do.
quotes: He was not powerful. He was terrified. His vision could not survive contact with arithmetic, everyone was about to watch it happen, and the only move fear left him was to make the person holding the numbers sit down.
Each was afraid of being found out. Each had learned the safest place to hide fear is behind confidence, because nobody checks the person who seems sure.
Confidence and competence look exactly alike from the outside. In the few seconds it takes to form an impression of someone, there is no way to tell them apart.
When someone junior flinches, nothing happens. When the most powerful person in the building does, everyone below rearranges themselves around it, and the whole company starts softening the truth.
A frightened boss cannot stand the person who sees what he misses, so he takes the deck, kills the forecast, and tells the truth to sit down. The secure one keeps her close.
Fear wants agreement, because agreement never exposes it. Confidence can stand to be corrected.
Their fear becomes your fear, and you carry it long after they are gone.
